title: Speed up of passive tracers in mixtures with active chemical reactions
authors: Filipe C. Thewes, Chengjie Luo, David Zwicker
abstract: Diffusivity of passive tracers in complex mixtures is widely relevant for industrial applications and for probing biological systems. Interactions with the surrounding medium typically generate a drag force that suppresses tracer diffusion, although self-propulsion can accelerate tracers via active fluctuations. Similar effects are not understood in mixtures with particle conversion and exchange, although these are particularly relevant in biological contexts, where actively driven reactions prevail. By studying a thermodynamically consistent model of chemical reactions in mixtures, we show that reactions provide an additional relaxation pathway that suppresses interaction-induced memory, reducing the drag on tracers and restoring their diffusivity toward the value expected in the absence of solutes. Moreover, active reactions generate nonequilibrium fluctuations that can push tracer diffusivity beyond this limit, an effect we confirm with particle-based simulations. Our results identify chemical activity as a distinct route to controlling mass transport and offer a framework for interpreting microrheology experiments in chemically active mixtures.
summary: This work analyzes how chemical reactions modify the diffusion of passive tracers in mixtures. Theoretically, it shows that while passive reactions slightly restore diffusion, active reactions introduce non-equilibrium fluctuations that can actively speed up the tracers. The findings establish chemical activity as a controllable mechanism for manipulating mass transport in soft matter and biological contexts.
main_problem: The paper investigates how chemical reactions, particularly active ones, influence the diffusion and mass transport of passive tracer particles in complex mixtures.
main_result: Active chemical reactions can significantly enhance the tracer diffusivity beyond the limits imposed by passive interactions, an effect attributed to non-equilibrium fluctuations.
method: The study combines theoretical path-integral methods (Martin-Siggia-Rose action) with particle-based Brownian dynamics simulations.
model_or_system: The system models a multicomponent mixture containing passive tracers coupled to solute particles undergoing both passive and active chemical reactions within a solvent bath.
key_observables: Mean Square Displacement (MSD), tracer diffusivity ($D_t$), and the deviation ($\delta$) of $D_t$ from the bare diffusivity ($D_0$).
important_parameters: Reaction-diffusion length scales ($\ell_{	ext{pass}}, \ell_{	ext{tot}}$), density ($ho$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical analysis relies on approximations like the saddle-point method and linearizing the free energy functional; simulations assume specific interaction potentials (Lennard-Jones).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the components (tracers, solutes, reactions) and show that diffusivity enhancement ($D/D_0$) is non-monotonic and maximized at intermediate reaction length scales when active fluctuations are present.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving equations for density fields and tracer dynamics, calculates the diffusivity correction ($\delta$) for passive and active cases, and confirms these predictions using detailed Brownian dynamics simulations.
why_interesting: The work provides a quantitative framework for understanding how non-equilibrium driving forces (chemical activity) can fundamentally alter transport properties, which has implications for understanding energy dissipation and fluctuation-driven dynamics in complex physical systems.
